At last I’ve found the time to write part 2. Back at work after Chinese New Year, I went straight into a conference deadline, and that frazzled feeling from my PhD days came rushing back. How nostalgic -_-! Lesson learned: when I write a two-parter, I shouldn’t leave too long between the parts. A train of thought only has so much momentum.

Anyway, let’s pick up where we left off.

Part 1 is here:

A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 1

Blindness separates us from things but deafness from people.

— Immanuel Kant

As I’ve said before, acoustics is a branch of physics, a natural science through and through. Psychoacoustics, a branch of acoustics, is the bridge between physics and people: it delivers sound to the brain through that precision sensor, the ear. Because it is physics, it is objective; because the brain is involved, it is subjective. So this article, too, follows those two broad lines: objective and subjective.

1. The physical world: objective evaluation

There’s a rough-and-ready correspondence:

Acoustics: sound pressure level

Psychoacoustics: A-weighted sound pressure level

We all know that the level of a sound is measured as sound pressure level in decibels (dB); in acoustics, that much is common ground. In psychoacoustics, a human listener is involved, and since the ear is less sensitive to low frequencies, the low end is attenuated. The result is the A-weighted sound pressure level, written dB(A). A-weighting was first proposed by Fletcher, whom we met in part 1.

Besides A-weighted SPL, the commonly used psychoacoustic metrics are:

loudness, sharpness, roughness and fluctuation strength. Which raises the question: what on earth are these?

  1. Loudness

As the name suggests, loudness is the psychoacoustic metric for how strong we perceive a sound’s intensity to be [1]. Note: sound intensity, not sound pressure, as Wikipedia has it [Loudness - Wikipedia].

Wikipedia is funny: the Chinese article says sound intensity, while the English one says sound pressure outright.

Put simply, sound intensity = sound pressure × particle velocity, so the two are not the same thing. We tend to know sound pressure well and particle velocity and sound intensity hardly at all, yet both quantities matter enormously, in theory and in practice. I’ll cover them in detail in a later article (promise).

Because of the particular anatomy of the ear, sounds of equal intensity but different frequency are perceived as differently loud. Look at the red curves between 10 and 1,000 Hz in the figure below (the x-axis is frequency in hertz): the lower the frequency, the higher the sound pressure level needed to reach the same loudness. On the threshold curve, the difference in SPL between 20 Hz and 1,000 Hz is as much as 70 dB or so. In other words, in this range, the lower the frequency, the less sensitive our hearing.

Because of these properties of hearing, loudness depends on frequency. Before we can derive loudness, we need loudness level.

For a plane wave arriving from the front (a very strict condition, mind you: when it isn’t met, the equal-loudness contours above no longer apply), loudness level is referenced to the SPL of a 1 kHz pure tone. If a 500 Hz pure tone sounds as loud to a listener as a 1 kHz tone at 50 dB, then the 500 Hz tone has a loudness level of 50 phon; the phon is the unit of loudness level. In the figure above, extending this across the whole frequency range gives one complete curve, and repeating it for 1 kHz tones at different levels gives the family of curves up the vertical axis. A 1 kHz tone at 40 dB is defined as having a loudness of 1 sone. When frequency is expressed on the Bark scale, loudness depends not only on frequency but also on the temporal envelope.

Look at the vertical red line in the figure. A 50 Hz pure tone at 50 dB has a loudness level of 20 phon, or 0.15 sone (equivalent to 20 dB at 1 kHz); at 110 dB, its loudness level rises to 100 phon, or 64 sone.

I won’t go any further into loudness calculation here; for the details, see chapter 8 of the psychoacoustics bible [1].

2. Other psychoacoustic metrics:

Sharpness describes an aspect of tone color, namely how sharp a sound is, and is calculated from loudness;

Roughness can be described as a parameter of a sound’s temporal masking pattern and depends on how fast the signal changes over time. In the auto industry, it can be used to judge whether a sound is “sporty”;

Fluctuation strength is defined much like roughness. The main difference is that it peaks at a modulation frequency of 4 Hz (roughness peaks at 70 Hz), which resembles the fluctuation of the waveform in speech. Four hertz also roughly matches the number of syllables we utter per second, which is why the auditory system is most sensitive to modulation at 4 Hz [2].

2. The human world: subjective evaluation

Psychoacoustic metrics are all derived from human judgments, that is, from subjective listening experiments. Before any experiment, the participants’ hearing has to be tested: audiometry. In short, pure tones at different frequencies are played, getting louder (or quieter), and you press a button the moment you can just hear the tone (or can just no longer hear it); the SPL at that moment is recorded. Below is the audiogram I had taken when I’d just started my PhD. You can see that below 4 kHz, my left ear (blue) needs a higher SPL than my right (red): the left ear is a little deafer. As for the two horizontal lines: below the yellow one, you get a yellow card; below the red one, a red card. So my left ear is poor between 500 and 1,500 Hz, and at 1,500 Hz in particular, I can’t hear anything below 30 dB at all! I was pretty glum when I saw it. So young, and already… Then I turned to look at the curve of the friend doing the experiment with me, and back at mine: not too bad! This Mr. C. Hell’s audiogram was a disaster. Later I found out he played guitar in a rock band…

That said, audiometry has a fairly large margin of error; test again the next day and you might get a completely different result. So if your results look bad, don’t panic. Just don’t rock out too hard ;-)

After audiometry, participants go into the listening lab (or a quiet room). In the picture below you can see loudspeakers that play back the test signals; headphones can be used too, of course.

Methods of subjective evaluation generally fall into the following categories [2]:

1. Random access

The participant listens to six sounds, A to F, and ranks them by sound quality from best (1) to worst (6) by dragging each sound to the corresponding number. Each sample can be replayed as often as the participant likes.

2. Semantic differential

The participant picks the words that best match how a sound strikes them.

3. Category scaling (I couldn’t find a good Chinese term for this one)

The participant rates each sound sample using a set of given words, each tied to a range of numerical values.

4. Magnitude estimation

Given the magnitude of a reference signal, the participant estimates the magnitude of another sound.

Other common methods include yes–no, 2AFC and 3AFC tasks [3]. TU Berlin has developed WhisPER, a MATLAB toolbox for listening tests that covers all the common methods [4].

So, once the listening test is done, how do you make sense of the data? Congratulations, you’ve just stepped through the blissful gates of statistics! To borrow from a Tang-dynasty poem: once you enter the house of statistics, deep as the sea, acoustics will pass you by like a stranger. For that part, please read someone else’s column on statistics, because I can’t do it =_=.

3. Sound quality

Sound quality is, as the name says, the quality of a sound. Jian Kang defines it in his book as follows [5]:

...the term sound quality describes the perception of the adequacy (Blauert and Jekosch, 1997), suitability (Guski, 1997), or desirability (Västfjäll and Kleiner, 2002) of a sound attached to the technical object emitting it.

In recent years, even as noise levels have come down quite low, people have found that the noise still gets on their nerves. Hence our discussion of psychoacoustics above, from both the objective and the subjective side. Now that manufacturing has hit a plateau, sound quality has gradually moved into the part of a product that consumers notice. In the auto industry, sound quality is a very important product attribute. Just how fine-grained does automotive sound quality get? A friend of mine at Mercedes-Benz headquarters does nothing but design reversing beeps. Besides the auto industry, construction, urban planning, white goods and other sectors all deal with sound quality problems and research. Sound quality engineering usually starts from a predefined target, which is reached by adjusting the physical properties of the sound.

Subjective evaluation is an indispensable part of assessing sound quality, and subjective evaluation naturally means human participants. But often it isn’t practical to have people listen to the sounds in question. For one thing, listening tests take time and effort; for another, once people have listened, that’s it: nothing is recorded, so there’s nothing to feed into further objective calculation and evaluation. Binaural technology solves this problem. From a binaural recording, you can easily calculate any physical quantity or psychoacoustic metric. And by recording several sound events to be evaluated and then bringing people into the listening lab, you can run several listening tests with the same group of people, under better-controlled conditions: everyone listens and rates in the same quiet environment.

So let’s take a closer look at binaural hearing.

4. The bridge between physics and people: binaural hearing

I mentioned binaural hearing in the previous psychoacoustics article; it has developed rapidly since 1960. The star of the story is today’s cover model, the artificial head, also called a dummy head or head and torso simulator, and in German, Kunstkopf. Sound samples are recorded with the artificial head for later calculation or listening tests. The principle isn’t complicated. On the outside, it’s a head with ears (if you’re feeling lazy, you can skip the rest of the face) on top of an upper torso; at the end of each ear canal sits a microphone, mimicking human binaural hearing. On its way to the microphones, sound is reflected, diffracted and set resonating by the torso, head, pinnae and ear canals. It’s the two ears, together with all these propagation effects, that let us localize and perceive sound. Of course, the actual perceiving is done by the big boss backstage: the brain. All these effects are captured in one magical function, the famous head-related transfer function, or HRTF. The free-field HRTF is calculated as follows:

Now look at what is recorded when a loudspeaker is placed to the left of the artificial head:

Imagine all you have is a sound recorded with a single microphone. How do you give your listeners a sense of space? Going further, how do you place that sound 30° to the front left of the listener? This is where the HRTF comes into its own. Convolve the mono signal with a set of HRTFs measured at 30° front left, listen on headphones, and you’ll be amazed: the sound seems to come from roughly that very spot. There are several large HRTF databases:

  • RWTH (Institute of Technical Acoustics)

  • LISTEN HRTF DATABASE

  • interface.cipic.ucdavis.edu

  • FIU DSP Lab, Anthropometric Measurements of HRTFs

  • Odeon, HRTF - Odeon

  • MIT, HRTF Measurements of a KEMAR Dummy-Head Microphone

HRTFs are usually measured at angles all around the artificial head, at various resolutions (1–5°). HRTFs and artificial heads have made both subjective and objective psychoacoustic evaluation far easier. But each has its limitations. An artificial head is built to the dimensions of an “average” human head, and an average, by definition, doesn’t represent any one individual. The downside is that the reflections, diffraction and resonances captured in an HRTF measured on an artificial head don’t exactly match what happens on a particular person. The HRTF is therefore not accurate, and the perceived sense of space can be off. That is why research on individualized HRTFs has taken off in recent years, for example by Professor Janina Fels at RWTH.

Binaural technology has a wide range of practical applications. Here are a few examples.

Back to the auto industry: artificial heads can be used for binaural transfer path analysis (binaural TPA). The figure below, for example, shows the paths by which tire noise reaches the driver’s two ears. This can inform sound design, making the sound that reaches the ears less annoying.

Combined with auralization, they are used to evaluate indoor acoustic environments and sound quality.

Echolocation for blind people. Echolocation is an instinct in some animals: they emit a sound and locate objects from the echoes that come back.

Recently, researchers have been studying how to combine virtual reality and binaural technology to help blind people locate and identify obstacles from the reflections of tongue clicks.

I’ll cover the technology behind binaural reproduction separately, in a future series on auralization.

Afterword

Done at last. Phew. Three days of writing, at least three intense hours a day of reading papers, hunting for images (and photoshopping them) and typing, and before I knew it, it was 8:30 on Sunday evening. Time to pack up and brace myself for dreaded Monday!

I recently came across an exchange between the two titans of acoustics. After Rayleigh published The Theory of Sound, Helmholtz wrote two reviews of it (yes, a book report can get you into Nature, so if you’ve finished reading this article, go write yours!). The last sentence of the second one really struck me:

“...Lord Rayleigh certainly deserves the thanks of all physicists and students of physics. He has rendered them a great service by what he has done hitherto. But I believe I am speaking in the name of all of them if I express the hope, that the difficulties of that which yet remains still incite him to crown his work by completing it.”
Lord Rayleigh’s Theory of Sound [a review by Hermann von Helmholtz, Nature 19, 117–118 (Dec. 12, 1878)]

These lines sum up what Helmholtz thought after reading the book, and it comes down to two things:

Recognition and thanks.

Yes, that’s all. One scientist to another, with no complicated personal feelings mixed in. I’m moved by how objective and pure great scientists can be about scientific work. It is exactly this attitude and generosity of spirit that spread the two masters’ work so widely, that still benefits those who came after them, and that keeps pushing acoustics forward.

References

[1] Zwicker, Eberhard, and Hugo Fastl. Psychoacoustics: Facts and Models. Vol. 22. Springer Science & Business Media, 2013.

[2] Blauert, Jens, ed. Communication Acoustics. Vol. 2. New York: Springer, 2005.

[3] Otto, Stefanie, and Stefan Weinzierl. “Comparative simulations of adaptive psychometric procedures.” Jahrestagung der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Akustik (2009): 1276–1279.

[4] WhisPER. A MATLAB toolbox for performing quantitative and qualitative listening tests.

[5] Kang, Jian, and Brigitte Schulte-Fortkamp, eds. Soundscape and the Built Environment. CRC Press, 2018.

[6] Janina Fels. RWTH course: Medical Acoustics.

[7] Vorländer, Michael. Auralization: Fundamentals of Acoustics, Modelling, Simulation, Algorithms and Acoustic Virtual Reality. Springer Science & Business Media, 2007.
